## Q4: Detect and Identify outliers

## select numeric variables
```{r}
c_var<-c(
   
  
   "Income" ,
   
   "Loan_Amount")   
  
# boxplot of outliers
data[c_var] |>
  scale() |>                                        
  # standardize: (x - mean) / sd
  as.data.frame() |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Boxplots of numerical variables", x = NULL, y = NULL)



```
 
 
# detection using 1.5 IQR
```{r}
detect_outliers_IQR<- function(x){
 Q1<- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm=TRUE)
 Q3<- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm=TRUE)
 IQR<-Q3-Q1
 lower<-Q1-1.5*IQR
 upper<-Q3+1.5*IQR
 which(x<lower|x>upper)}
  
```



# confirmation of outlier detection
# count outliers
```{r}
  
outlier_count <- sapply(data[c_var],
                        function(x) length(detect_outliers_IQR(x)))
outs <- outlier_count[outlier_count > 0]

if (length(outs) == 0) {
  cat("No outliers detected in any numerical variable.\n")
} else {
  cat("Outliers detected:\n")
  print(outs)
}
```


### get mode function
```{r}
get_mode<-function (x){
  ux<-unique(na.omit(x))
  ux[which.max(
    tabulate(match(x, ux)))]}

  cat("mode=",get_mode(data$Loan_Amount),"\n")
```

## replace with the mode (iterate until stable)
```{r}
max_iter   <- 10
converged  <- FALSE

for (i in seq_len(max_iter)) {
  n_replaced <- 0
  for (var in c_var) {
    idx <- detect_outliers_IQR(data[[var]])
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      mode_val <- get_mode(data[[var]])
      data[[var]][idx] <- mode_val
      n_replaced <- n_replaced + length(idx)
    }
  }
  cat(sprintf("Pass %d: replaced %d value(s)\n", i, n_replaced))
  if (n_replaced == 0) { converged <- TRUE; break }
}

if (!converged) warning("Outlier replacement did not converge in ", max_iter, " passes.")
```

## Q10: compute skewness
```{r}
library(e1071)

sk <- sapply(data[num_var], skewness)
# using table view
skew_df <- data.frame(
 Variable  = names(sk),
  Skewness  = round(as.numeric(sk), 3),
 
  Direction = ifelse(sk > 0, 
                     "Right-skewed (positive)",
              ifelse(sk < 0,
                     "Left-skewed (negative)", "Symmetric")),
 
  Magnitude = ifelse(abs(sk) < 0.5, 
                     "Low / roughly symmetric",
```

- The skewness of Income is 0.713 and of Loan_Amount is 0.749. Both are positive and fall in the 0.5–1 range, indicating moderate right-skewness. This means the majority of applicants have relatively modest incomes and take out smaller loans, while a smaller number of high-income applicants take much larger loans, producing a long right tail. The result is consistent with mean > median for both variables and with the shape of their histograms.

```{r}
    x_chr %in% c("no",  "n", "0", "false", "f") ~ "No",
    x_chr %in% c("yes", "y", "1", "true",  "t") ~ "Yes",

  ),
```

# SECTION D: Visualization
## Q13. Histogram of `Credit_Score`.  and Description of  the shape of the distribution.
```{r}
x <- data$Credit_Score

## summary values
m_mean   <- mean(x)
m_median <- median(x)

## mode (most frequent value)
get_mode <- function(v) {
  v <- v[!is.na(v)]
  ux <- unique(v)
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(v, ux)))]
}
m_mode <- get_mode(x)

ggplot(data, aes(x = Credit_Score)) +
  
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = m_mean,   colour = "red",   linewidth = 1, linetype = "solid") +
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = m_median, colour = "blue",  linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = m_mode,   colour = "green", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  
  annotate("text", x = m_mean,   y = Inf, label = "Mean",   vjust = 2, colour = "red") +
  
  annotate("text", x = m_median, y = Inf, label = "Median", vjust = 4, colour = "blue") +
  
  annotate("text", x = m_mode,   y = Inf, label = "Mode",   vjust = 6, colour = "green") +
  
  labs(title = "Distribution of Credit_Score",
       x = "Credit Score", y = "Frequency") +
  
  theme_minimal()

```


### Description of the shape
The histogram of Credit_Score shows a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped (unimodal) distribution, with the three central-tendency lines confirming the shape:

- Mean (red, ≈ 651.7), Median (blue, ≈ 650.0), and Mode (green) all sit close together near the centre of the distribution. When mean ≈ median ≈ mode, the distribution is approximately symmetric — a classic signature of normality.

- Shape: Bell-shaped, unimodal — a single clear peak around 640–700, with frequencies tapering off evenly on both sides.

- Spread: Scores range from 450 to 820, standard deviation ≈ 109.

- Skewness: Near zero (previously computed ≈ –0.05) — the left and right tails are balanced.

- Outliers: None — the tails fade smoothly, and no isolated bars appear far from the centre.

- Modality: Unimodal — one peak, no secondary clusters.

### What the lines tell us visually:

- If the mean line sits to the right of the median, the distribution is right-skewed.

- If the mean line sits to the left of the median, it is left-skewed.

- the distribution is left-skewed

### Conclusion (one-liner)
- The histogram of Credit_Score is left-skewed (negatively skewed) and unimodal, centred around 650 with a range of 450–820. The mean line sits to the left of the median line, confirming that the longer tail lies on the left side of the distribution. No outliers are present.

```{r}

agg <- aggregate(Income ~ Loan_Approved, data = data,
                 FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), min = min(x),
                                     median = median(x),
                                     mean = mean(x), max = max(x)))

do.call(data.frame, agg)
```

## What the boxplot reveals
### Complete separation by income. 
- The two boxes do not overlap at all — the highest income in the "No" group (42,000) is still below the lowest in the "Yes" group (44,000). Every approved applicant earns more than every non-approved applicant, so income perfectly discriminates approval status in this dataset.

### Much higher median for approved. 
- The median income of the "Yes" group (72,000) is roughly 2.5× that of the "No" group (28,500). The means tell the same story — 77,273 vs 28,850, a ratio of about 2.7×.

- mSimilar spread, different location. Both boxes have comparable IQR widths — the variability in income is similar across groups, so it is the location (central tendency) that differs, not the dispersion.

### Different ranges.

- "No" is tightly bounded between 17,000 and 42,000 (median 28,500).

- "Yes" stretches from 44,000 up to 135,000 (median 72,000) — the approved group contains the entire high-income tail.

### Few or no outliers.
- The whiskers extend to the extremes because the data is bounded and evenly spread — no isolated points lie beyond the fences.

# Q21. Should the scaling parameters be computed on the full dataset or only the training set? Justify.


### Only on the training set. The scaling parameters (mean, standard deviation, min, max — whichever you use) must be computed exclusively from the training data, then applied to the test data (and any future data).

####Justification
- 1. Data leakage (the main reason):
If you compute the mean and standard deviation using the full dataset (training + test), information from the test set "leaks" into the training process. The model indirectly sees the test set's distribution before it is supposed to. This makes the test set no longer a fair, unseen sample.

- The result: your evaluation metrics (RMSE, accuracy, AUC, etc.) become overly optimistic and do not reflect how the model would perform on genuinely new data.

- 2. Simulating real-world deployment:
In production, when a new observation arrives, you will not have the future dataset to recompute scaling parameters. You must use the parameters learned during training. So the training pipeline should mimic this: compute parameters once on the training data, freeze them, and reuse them for everything else.

- 3. Preserving the test set as a proxy for unseen data:
The whole point of a test set is to estimate out-of-sample performance. If the test set influenced the scaling, it is no longer "out-of-sample" with respect to preprocessing — the model was tuned (even if only slightly) to it.

- 4. Consistency across splits:
If you scale the training and test sets separately (each with its own mean/std), the two sets live in different feature spaces. A value of 1.0 in the training set means something different from 1.0 in the test set. This breaks the model's assumptions.

# SECTION G: SVM Classification
***Q23. Train an SVM classifier with a linear kernel on the scaled training data. Report the model summary.
```{r}
# Define features
features <- c("Age", "Income", "Credit_Score", "Loan_Amount", "Employment_Years")
x_train <- train[, features]
y_train <- train$Loan_Approved

# Scale features
preProc <- preProcess(x_train, method = c("center", "scale"))
x_train_scaled <- predict(preProc, x_train)
x_test_scaled <- predict(preProc, test[, features])

# Linear SVM
svm_linear <- svm(x = x_train_scaled, y = y_train, kernel = "linear", cost = 1, scale = FALSE)
summary(svm_linear)
```

# Q26. Compare the performance of the linear kernel vs the RBF kernel. Which performs better and why?
```{r}
# ---- 1. Predictions from both models ----
pred_linear <- predict(svm_linear, x_test_scaled)
pred_rbf    <- predict(svm_rbf,    x_test_scaled)

# ---- 2. Force identical factor levels ("No"/"Yes") ----
actual      <- factor(as.character(test$Loan_Approved), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
pred_linear <- factor(as.character(pred_linear),        levels = c("No", "Yes"))
pred_rbf    <- factor(as.character(pred_rbf),           levels = c("No", "Yes"))

# ---- 3. Confusion matrices ----
cm_linear <- confusionMatrix(pred_linear, actual,
                             positive = "Yes", mode = "prec_recall")
cm_rbf    <- confusionMatrix(pred_rbf,    actual,
                             positive = "Yes", mode = "prec_recall")

# ---- 4. Compare ----
cat("Linear kernel\n"); print(cm_linear$table)
cat("\nRBF kernel\n");  print(cm_rbf$table)

cat("\n--- Metrics ---\n")
cat(sprintf("Linear  Accuracy: %.4f | F1: %.4f | Sensitivity: %.4f | Specificity: %.4f\n",
            cm_linear$overall["Accuracy"],
            cm_linear$byClass["F1"],
            cm_linear$byClass["Sensitivity"],
            cm_linear$byClass["Specificity"]))

cat(sprintf("RBF     Accuracy: %.4f | F1: %.4f | Sensitivity: %.4f | Specificity: %.4f\n",
            cm_rbf$overall["Accuracy"],
            cm_rbf$byClass["F1"],
            cm_rbf$byClass["Sensitivity"],
            cm_rbf$byClass["Specificity"]))
```

# Q29. Compute the following metrics for the SVM model:
 Accuracy
 Precision
 Recall (Sensitivity)
 F1-Score
 Specificity
```{r}
# (uses the best SVM from Q25 and the scaled test data)

pred_svm <- predict(best_svm, x_test_scaled)
pred_svm <- factor(as.character(pred_svm), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
actual   <- factor(as.character(test$Loan_Approved), levels = c("No", "Yes"))

cm_svm <- confusionMatrix(pred_svm, actual,
                          positive = "Yes",
                          mode     = "prec_recall")   # ensures Precision/Recall/F1 exist

print(cm_svm$table)

# ---- 2. Pull metrics directly from the table (always works) ----
TP <- cm_svm$table["Yes", "Yes"]
TN <- cm_svm$table["No",  "No"]
FP <- cm_svm$table["Yes", "No"]
FN <- cm_svm$table["No",  "Yes"]

accuracy_svm    <- (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
precision_svm   <- TP / (TP + FP)
recall_svm      <- TP / (TP + FN)          # Sensitivity
specificity_svm <- TN / (TN + FP)
f1_svm          <- 2 * precision_svm * recall_svm /
                   (precision_svm + recall_svm)

# ---- 3. Print each metric explicitly ----
cat("===== SVM Performance Metrics =====\n")
cat(sprintf("Accuracy    : %.4f\n", accuracy_svm))
cat(sprintf("Precision   : %.4f\n", precision_svm))
cat(sprintf("Recall      : %.4f\n", recall_svm))
cat(sprintf("F1-Score    : %.4f\n", f1_svm))
cat(sprintf("Specificity : %.4f\n", specificity_svm))
cat("====================================\n")

# ---- 4. (Optional) cross-check against caret's byClass ----
print(cm_svm$byClass)
```

```{r}
)
```

# Q32. Tune the following hyperparameters using grid search or random search:
 `nrounds`
 `max_depth`
 `eta` (learning rate)
 `subsample`
 `colsample_bytree`
```{r}
library(caret)
library(xgboost)

# Feature set
features <- c("Age", "Income", "Credit_Score", "Loan_Amount", "Employment_Years")

x_train_mat <- as.matrix(train[, features])
y_train_num <- as.integer(train$Loan_Approved) - 1L
dtrain      <- xgb.DMatrix(x_train_mat, label = y_train_num)

# Small grid
grid <- expand.grid(
  nrounds          = c(50, 100),
  max_depth        = c(3, 6),
  eta              = c(0.1, 0.3),
  subsample        = 0.8,
  colsample_bytree = 0.8
)

results <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:nrow(grid)) {
  g <- grid[i, ]
  cv <- xgb.cv(
    params = list(
      objective        = "binary:logistic",
      eval_metric      = "logloss",
      max_depth        = g$max_depth,
      eta              = g$eta,
      subsample        = g$subsample,
      colsample_bytree = g$colsample_bytree
    ),
    data    = dtrain,
    nrounds = g$nrounds,
    nfold   = 3,
    verbose = 0
  )
  results <- rbind(results,
                   cbind(g, logloss = min(cv$evaluation_log$test_logloss_mean)))
}

results <- results[order(results$logloss), ]
print(results)
```

```{r}
# ============================================================

auc_xgb_num <- as.numeric(auc_xgb)

  Metric  = c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1-Score",
              "Specificity", "AUC"),
  SVM     = round(c(accuracy_svm, precision_svm, recall_svm,
                    f1_svm, specificity_svm, auc_svm_num), 4),
  XGBoost = round(c(accuracy_xgb, precision_xgb, recall_xgb,
                    f1_xgb, specificity_xgb, auc_xgb_num), 4)
)

# Optional: highlight which model wins each row

                     ifelse(comparison$XGBoost > comparison$SVM, "XGBoost",
```

## Q40. Which model performs better on this dataset? Justify with evidence.

# Both models perform equally well. There is no measurable difference on the test set — every metric is identical at 1.00.

However, if a single model must be chosen, the linear SVM is the better practical choice.


- conclusion:
SVM and XGBoost perform identically on this dataset — both achieve 100% accuracy, precision, recall, F1, specificity, and AUC. Because the target is a simple threshold on Credit_Score, the linear SVM is the preferred model: it matches XGBoost on every metric while being simpler, faster, and easier to interpret. XGBoost's extra complexity provides no benefit and only adds unnecessary risk of overfitting on future data.
